en: Petavatthu,
Mahāvagga 2.
The Story of the Serīsaka Ghosts
“Listen to how the encounter between the yakkha and the merchants occurred,
and what was said by each to the other.”
Listen all to this well-spoken word:
That king named Pāyāsi,
who was renowned and had attained companionship with the earth-dwellers;
Thus, rejoicing in his own celestial mansion,
the non-human being addressed the human being:
"In the crooked forest, in a place uninhabited by humans..."
In a wilderness devoid of water and lacking food,
in the midst of a forest path difficult to traverse,
people lost their way through crooked fears.
Here there are no fruits that consist of roots, nor is there any grasping;
whence, then, could there be food? Save for dust and sand.
With those [fires] that are hot and terrible,
this parched skull is like a heated vessel not made of iron—
equal to the world beyond.
This is the ancient dwelling place of hunters,
a region of land that has become desolate.
Now, for what reason do you— ?
“Desiring what have you entered this place so suddenly and with such arrogance—
out of greed, fear, or perhaps sheer delusion?”
“Caravan leaders from Magadha and Aṅga,
having loaded their various wares,
set out for the lands of Sindhu and Sovīra.”
Seeking wealth and desiring gain,
they do not endure thirst even by day,
looking instead for compassion from their drivers.
"Come all with this speed;
we have set out on the road at night, at an improper time.
We are poorly traveled and have strayed from the path."
Blinded and lost in the wilderness,
in the midst of a difficult path through the forest,
we do not know the direction, our minds utterly bewildered.
And having seen this, never before seen—
the most excellent celestial mansion and yourself, O yakkha—
we shall live on, hoping for even more than this.
“Having seen this, she was thrilled, joyful, and elated.
“The shore of the ocean, this beauty,
the path through the reed-thicket, and the road with its thorny tracks;”
But rivers and mountain passes are difficult to traverse;
go forth in various directions for the sake of wealth.
Having invaded the conquered territories of others, [enjoy them].
“O dear ones, while looking at these people from Verañjā, tell us what you have heard or even seen that is wonderful.”
“Even more wonderful than this, O Prince,
is that which we have neither heard nor seen;
it is entirely beyond the human realm of the past.”
Having seen this, we are not satiated by your peerless beauty.
From the lotus pond, many garlands and numerous white lotuses flow through the air.
These trees are always laden with fruit,
and their fragrance wafts forth most sweetly;
they stand raised up like pillars of beryl.
And the long rafters are of crystal;
these pillars, radiant with light, are made of emerald together with rubies.
Upon those [palaces] stands this excellent celestial mansion, possessing a thousand pillars and incomparable majesty,
interspersed with jewels and a golden altar.
And well-covered with cloths of refined gold;
this palace, made of highly polished Jambunada gold,
is provided with stairs and a terrace.
Firm, charming, and well-composed,
exceedingly capable of deep reflection and pleasing;
in that jewel-like place, there is abundant food and drink.
Surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs,
resounded by the music of muraja drums, ālambara lutes,
and other instruments, you were honored with salutations and hymns of praise.
Thus you rejoice, awakening the throngs of women,
in this most excellent and delightful celestial mansion and palace;
inconceivable, endowed with every virtue.
Like King Vessavaṇa in the Naḷinī grove—
were you a deity dwelling in the water, a yakkha,
or perhaps a lord of gods who had become a human?
The merchant caravan leaders asked him:
"Tell us, what is your name, O yakkha?
"I am a yakkha named Serīsaka," he replied.
"Like one protected on a path through the wilderness, I guard this region,
obeying the word of King Vessavaṇa."
“Was this obtained by chance, or born of transformation,
or was it made by yourself, or given by the gods?
The merchant caravan leaders are asking you this.”
“How was this delightful thing obtained by you?
“It was not obtained by supernatural power, nor born of transformation;
it was not made by myself, nor indeed given by the gods.”
“Through blameless deeds and meritorious acts,
this delightful thing has been obtained by me.
“What was your vow, and what was your holy life?”
“Of what well-performed deed is this the result?
The merchants and caravan leaders ask you:
‘How was this celestial mansion obtained by you?’”
“Mamaṁ pāyāsī” was the name by which I was known when I ruled the kingdom of the Kosalans—
a nihilist, miserly, and evil-natured.
And at that time I was an annihilationist.
But there was also the ascetic Kumārakassapa,
who was highly learned, an eloquent speaker, and sublime.
Then he spoke this discourse on Dhamma to me,
dispelling my views and perplexities.
Having heard that discourse on Dhamma from him, I—
I shall declare myself a lay follower;
I shall abstain from taking life and avoid what is not given in the world.
I did not drink intoxicants, nor did I speak falsehood;
I was content with my own wife.
That was my vow, and that was my holy life.
“This is the result of that well-performed deed;
by those very same blameless and meritorious actions,
this celestial mansion has been obtained by me.”
“Truly, as the wise men have said,
the words of the learned are not otherwise:
wherever one who performs meritorious deeds goes, [there he prospers].”
There and there the seeker of desires rejoices;
wherever there is sorrow and lamentation,
killing, bondage, and affliction— there he rejoices.
“Wherever he goes, the one of evil karma is never released from the miserable states.
“The people were as if utterly bewildered.”
"In this very moment, O Prince, for this people and for you as well,
why indeed has there been such distress?"
“O dear ones, these Sirīsa groves emit divine,
fragrant, and sweet scents;
they waft throughout this celestial mansion.”
Having destroyed darkness both by day and by night—
yet even so, at the passing of these hundred years,
each single seed-pod bears fruit.
A hundred human years have passed since I was first reborn here in this body;
having seen five hundred such years elapse, I—
"O dear ones, standing in this celestial mansion,
I shall pass away due to the exhaustion of my lifespan and the exhaustion of my merit;
it is because of that very sorrow that I am distraught."
“How could such a person as he grieve,
having obtained an incomparable celestial mansion after a long time,
while others have been reborn only for a brief duration?”
“Those of little merit would surely grieve.
“What you say to me— that you speak kind words— is appropriate and worthy of my instruction.”
"And you, dear ones, being protected by me,
may go safely wherever you wish. "Having gone to the land of Sindhu-Sovīra,"
“Seeking wealth and aspiring for gain,
with our efforts fully directed toward generosity,
we shall achieve great sovereignty ourselves.”
“Do not treat me with contempt,
for whatever you say shall come to pass for all of you;
avoid all evil deeds.”
And resolve upon devotion to the Dhamma.
There is a lay follower in this Saṅgha,
who is learned and endowed with virtue and practice.
Faithful, generous, and kind,
discerning, contented, and wise—
one who understands should not speak falsely.
One should not intend to harm others;
one should not engage in divisive speech for the sake of creating discord;
rather, one should speak words that are gentle and kindly.
The person who is respectful, reverential, disciplined,
free from evil, and purified in higher virtue—
such a person [honors] both mother and father.
He supports them according to the Dhamma with noble conduct.
I believe that for the sake of his parents he seeks wealth, not for his own sake.
And he who, after the passing of his mother and father,
shall live the holy life inclined toward renunciation—
upright, free from crookedness, without guile, and without deceit.
One should not engage in trade by means of a false measure;
such a person, who performs deeds well done and stands firm in the Dhamma— how could he experience suffering?
It is for this reason that I have revealed myself;
therefore, O merchants, behold the Dhamma!
Otherwise, you would be reduced to ashes right here.
“Blinded and lost in the forest,
they were quickly rescued by another who was swift;
indeed, happy is the meeting with a true person.”
“What is his name, and what work does he do?
What is his designation, and what is his clan? We too, O yakkha, desire to see him.”
“Out of compassion for whom have you come here?
It is indeed a gain for him for whom you feel such longing.
“He who is the barber named Sambhava...”
"There is a lay follower who subsists on the fruit of the *koccha* tree; know him to be your own servant.
Do not despise him, for he is very kind."
“We know what you proclaim, O Yakkha,
yet we do not know that he is such as this;
we too shall honor him, O Yakkha.”
“Having heard your sublime words.
“Whatever people there are in this caravan—
whether young, old, or middle-aged;”
“May all those misers behold this celestial mansion and see the fruit of their meritorious deeds!
Thus they all there cried out, “I first! I first!”
Having placed that barber at their head,
they all supported themselves upon that celestial mansion,
just as the gods do upon Masakkasāra, the abode of Vāsava.
There, they all declared,
"I was here before," and they professed their status as lay followers;
they became abstainers from taking life.
In that world, they avoided taking what was not given;
they did not drink intoxicants nor speak falsehoods,
and they were content with their own wives.
There, they all said, "I was first," having declared their status as lay followers;
the caravan then departed, offering words of appreciation.
With the approval of the yakkha’s psychic power, they went again and again to the lands of the Sindhuvīras,
seeking wealth and desiring gain.
Having obtained their full rewards according to their efforts,
they returned safely to Pāṭaliputta;
having traveled to the Saṅgharama, they arrived in safety.
Accompanied by sons and wives,
joyful, wealthy, happy, and delighted,
they performed a magnificent festival of sovereignty.
They had a cell built for you at Serīsaka.
Such is the service of the truly good:
the cultivation of the qualities of the Dhamma is of great benefit.
"For the sake of one lay follower,
all beings indeed became happy.
This is the second *Serīsaka-peta-vatthu*.
The third recitation section.
